title: The Letter
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: The letter arrived on a Tuesday. Ordinary envelope, blue ballpoint, a hand she vaguely recognized. The postmark on the back was legible: Bristol, April 12. Below the current year, in smaller type, was a second date. It said: 2 April 2005. She was, at that year, twenty-three. The letter, when she opened it, was from her.

chapters.title: Postmark
chapters.body:
The letter arrived on a Tuesday.

It arrived, along with the small ordinary Tuesday post, in the small brass letterbox in the entrance hall of the building where Meredith Cole lived — a small brick building of four flats in Bristol, on a quiet street of Victorian terraces near the city centre, where she had lived for the last eight years. It arrived, from what she could tell in the small brief moment before she brought it upstairs, addressed by hand, in a hand she did not immediately recognize.

She was forty-four. She was, that Tuesday, home in the middle of the afternoon, because she worked from the small second bedroom of her flat as a freelance editor of academic manuscripts, and had been, at three o'clock, taking a small break to check the post and to make a cup of tea.

She had taken the letter and the two other pieces of post up to her flat, and had, at the small kitchen counter, put the kettle on. She had, waiting for the water, looked at the letter.

The envelope had been ordinary. It had been the standard white long envelope one bought at any small stationery shop. It had had, in the top-left corner, no return address. It had had, in the centre, her own name and current address written in a small careful cursive hand in blue ballpoint pen.

She had, on studying the writing for a moment, thought that the hand looked like her mother's.

She had, on further study, understood that it was not.

It had been slightly larger. It had been in blue rather than her mother's specific black. It had, in the small careful shape of certain letters — the specific loop of the *g* in her surname, the specific serif of the capital *M* in her first name — reminded her of someone else. Someone she could not, in the moment, immediately place.

She had turned the envelope over.

The postmark had been on the back flap. She had squinted at it. It had been a Bristol postmark. The date, in the small round stamp, had been legible: April 12.

The current year had been printed clearly.

Below the year, in a smaller line she had not, at first, been able to read, had been another date. She had held the envelope closer to the small window over the sink.

The second date had been legible.

It had said: *2 April 2005.*

She had, at the small kitchen counter, held the envelope for a moment.

She had thought, quickly: *misprint. The postal service had misprinted the year. It should have said the current year twice.*

She had thought, then: *some kind of postmark reused from an old stamp.*

She had thought, at last: *look at the address.*

She had looked at the front of the envelope again. Her name. Her current address on Alma Road. She had lived at Alma Road for eight years. In April 2005 — twenty-one years ago, when she had been twenty-three — she had lived at a small student flat on Gloucester Road, in the second year after her graduation.

The letter had been addressed to a flat she had not moved into for another thirteen years.

She had, at the counter, put the letter down slowly.

She had, for perhaps a full minute, done nothing.

The kettle had come to its boil. It had, with its small ordinary click, switched itself off. She had not moved to pour the water.

She had, at last, picked up the letter, and had walked to the small round dining table in the sitting room, and had sat down.

She had opened the envelope.

Inside had been a single sheet of white paper, folded in thirds. She had unfolded it.

The paper had had, at the top, no letterhead. It had had, in the top right corner, in the same small careful cursive hand as the envelope, a date.

The date had been *2 April 2005.*

Below the date, without any greeting or salutation, the letter had begun:

*Meredith,*

*I am writing this on the assumption that you will read it when you are forty-four. I am writing it on 2 April 2005. I am, at the moment of writing, twenty-three. This is not, I know, going to be an easy sentence for you to read. I am going to ask you to sit with it. I have thought about it for a long time. I am, in the specific small way you and I both understand these things, writing to myself.*

Meredith had, at the small round table, stopped reading.

She had put the letter down.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who did not entirely permit her rational mind to be overrun immediately, gotten up and had walked into the kitchen. She had poured the boiling water — which had, in the last several minutes, cooled slightly, but was still adequately hot — into a small teapot. She had let it steep. She had gone into the small bathroom and had washed her hands. She had returned to the kitchen. She had poured the tea into a small mug. She had carried the mug to the sitting room.

She had sat back down at the small round table.

She had read the letter again from the beginning.

*I am, in the specific small way you and I both understand these things, writing to myself.*

She had gone on.

*I do not know how this letter is arriving to you. I have not, as I write this, worked out the mechanism. I have only, over the last four months, come to understand that I can send it — that I can put a letter into a small postbox with your address on it, and that the letter will, in some way I do not understand, arrive at you. I have tested this. I have, in the last month, sent three small letters to test recipients: one to myself at the current address, which arrived; one to a friend at a specific address in London, which arrived; and one to you at Alma Road, Bristol, which — I am, at the time of writing, waiting to hear about. If this letter reaches you, that will be the confirmation.*

*You will, if you are still living at Alma Road when this arrives, understand that I have found the mechanism.*

*I am writing to warn you.*

Meredith had, at that word, felt a small definite cold pass through her.

She had, at the small round table, gone on reading.

*I know that on 2 April 2005 you have not yet, of course, done any of the things you have done between 2005 and whatever year you are receiving this. I know that from your perspective all of your adult decisions have already been made. You have, from your perspective, made them all yourself. You have made your career. You have made your relationships. You have made your home. I am not writing to argue with any of this. I am not writing to change any of it. I am writing to tell you that on the third of May in the year you receive this letter, you are going to make a small decision that will kill you within six weeks. I want to prevent this decision.*

*I do not know, from where I am, exactly what the decision is. I know only that it is small. That it will not, at the moment you make it, feel important. That it will feel like the small kind of decision you make many times a day without noticing. And that it will, over the following six weeks, cause you to die.*

*I know this because on the third of May 2005 I made the small decision that is going to kill me by the middle of June. I am writing this on 2 April, four days after having received a letter — a specific small letter written in a specific small handwriting I did not initially recognize — postmarked from 2049, from a woman who identified herself as me at eighty-eight. She had written to me to warn me. She had said that on 3 May 2005 I was going to make a small decision that would kill me. She had asked me to be careful.*

*I did not, when I received her letter, believe her.*

*I believed, on 2 April 2005, that the letter was a small elaborate hoax by a friend. I put it in a drawer. I did not think about it again. On 3 May 2005 I went, in the specific small way of a woman who did not know she was making a decision, to the pharmacy on Whiteladies Road to pick up a small prescription. I was, at the time, taking a specific antihistamine for a small case of hay fever. I had, on my ordinary route home, walked past a small building site where a small worker had, without warning, dropped a small brick from a scaffold. The brick had struck me on the back of the head. I had, over the following six weeks, developed a small slow subdural haematoma, which had been misdiagnosed as tension headaches, and which had, on 14 June 2005, produced a brief seizure in the small kitchen of my student flat that had killed me.*

*The elderly woman who wrote to me — the woman who is, I have to assume, some version of me who did not die at twenty-three — had warned me not to go to the pharmacy on 3 May. She had suggested a different route home. She had asked me to be careful of small building sites near tall buildings for the whole of that week. She had, in her letter, been specific about the exact hour and the exact street at which the brick would fall.*

*I did not believe her.*

*I did not believe her because the letter had come in a small ordinary envelope, in a hand that looked slightly like my mother's, and had made a claim that was, in the ordinary small careful understanding of the world, ridiculous. I had, at the time, been a rational woman of twenty-three who had been trained as an undergraduate in analytic philosophy, and I had, in my rational way, dismissed the letter as an obvious hoax.*

*I am writing to you now, in the last weeks of my life, to tell you what I wish I had done differently.*

Meredith had, at the small round table, understood something with a small quiet clarity.

She had understood that the letter she was holding had, according to its own claim, been written by a woman who had known she was going to die. That the woman was claiming, further, to have received a similar warning from an older woman, and to have ignored it. That she was writing, now, at twenty-three, in the last weeks of her life, to warn her forty-four-year-old self — some counterfactual version, some *other* version of herself who had somehow lived — about a small decision that was going to be made in the year of receipt, and that would kill her.

Meredith had understood, in the same small quiet clarity, that this was — in the ordinary careful understanding of the world — an obvious hoax.

Or a mistake.

Or the writing of a woman who was, in some specific small way, ill.

She had, at the small round table, permitted the possibility that it was a hoax to sit with her for a moment.

She had, in the specific small way of a woman who had been a freelance academic editor for eighteen years, considered the evidence.

She had considered the handwriting. The handwriting had been in a small careful hand that was, in the specific small way of certain features, familiar to her. It had had the specific loop of the *g* that her own hand had, throughout her twenties, had, before she had, in her early thirties, deliberately altered it because she had been told, at some workplace or other, that her *g* looked childish. She had not, in the last decade, written the *g* that way. She had not been able to write it that way now, without conscious effort.

She had considered the postmark. The postmark had been from Bristol, dated 2 April 2005. She had, in that period, been living in Bristol. She had, in April 2005, been twenty-three.

She had considered the small specific claim about the pharmacy on Whiteladies Road.

She had, at that consideration, stopped.

She had, at the small round table, remembered that in April 2005 she had, in fact, been taking a specific antihistamine for hay fever. She had, in the specific small way she had come to think of certain small facts of her past, remembered picking it up at the pharmacy on Whiteladies Road, because that had been the pharmacy she had used throughout her early twenties.

She had also remembered, in the specific small way one remembered small close-call moments from twenty years earlier, that on the third of May 2005, she had, on her ordinary walk home from that pharmacy, been almost hit by a falling brick from a small scaffolding site at the corner of Whiteladies and St Paul's Road.

She had not, of course, been hit. She had, at some point in the small quiet way of one's memory of one's own small close calls, understood that she had, that afternoon, been unusually fortunate. The brick had fallen, and she had, for reasons she had never entirely been able to identify, been standing perhaps three feet from where she would normally have been standing, and the brick had missed her by that three feet, and she had, in the specific small ordinary way of a person having a small close call, gone home and had had a cup of tea and had thought about it for perhaps an hour and had then, more or less, forgotten it.

She had, sitting at the small round table on a Tuesday in April at forty-four, remembered it.

She had understood, remembering it, that the letter's specific claim about the brick was correct.

She had understood, further, that the letter's claim about the pharmacy was correct.

She had understood, at last, that if she had not, on the third of May 2005, been standing three feet to the left of where she would ordinarily have been standing — for reasons she still could not identify — she would, according to the letter, have been struck on the head, and would, according to the letter, have died six weeks later.

She had, at the small round table, put down the letter, and had, for the first time in the twenty-one years since May of 2005, wondered what precisely had made her, that afternoon, stand three feet to the left.

She had, in the small quiet of her sitting room, been unable to remember.

chapters.title: The Decision
chapters.body:
The letter had continued for another two pages.

She had, on the following pages, read the specific small careful warnings her younger self had provided about the small decision that was, according to the letter, going to kill her in the current year.

The younger self — Meredith understood, on the second reading, that she was going to have to think of her that way, as a specific other person even though the letter was, in its own way, addressed from herself — had explained that she did not, from her position, know exactly what the decision was.

*I do not know,* the younger self had written, *what the decision looks like for you. It will look, from your perspective, like a small ordinary choice. I know only three things about it. I know that you will make it on the third of May. I know that, whatever it is, it will result in your death within six weeks. And I know that, from the older woman who wrote to me, she had made a similar small decision at forty-four, and had similarly not survived it. She had, in her letter to me, written that she believed the pattern would continue — that there was, in some sense, a specific small point in your forty-fourth year at which each version of you was, without your knowing it, coming to a small crossroads that would either kill you or would not.*

*The old woman said that she had, at eighty-eight, been the one version of you who had, on 3 May of her forty-fourth year, done something different. She did not remember what she had done. She had, over the sixty-five years since, not been able to reconstruct which small decision, of the many small decisions of her ordinary day, had been the one that had saved her.*

*She had written to warn me all the same. She had written in the hope that I could, by knowing the day, do something different — however small, however unlikely to matter. She had written because she had, at eighty-eight, understood that even a small warning was better than none.*

*I did not believe her.*

*I am writing to you now to warn you in the same way. I do not know what the decision is. I know only that it is on the third of May. I know only that it is small. I know only that if you do exactly what you would ordinarily have done that day, you will not survive it.*

*I ask you, on the third of May of the year you receive this, to do something different.*

*It does not matter what. Take a different route to the shops. Do not answer the telephone. Do not accept an invitation you would ordinarily have accepted. Cook something new for dinner. Do not, on that specific day, do anything you would have done without thinking about it.*

*This is the whole of my request.*

*I do not know if it will work. I have not, from where I am, any way of testing it. I know only that the older woman who wrote to me was, at eighty-eight, alive; and that I, at twenty-three, at the time of writing this, am dying; and that the difference between us was, so far as she could tell, the difference between having done the small ordinary thing on the third of May and having done the small different thing.*

*I love you. I love you, in the specific small careful way I have of loving myself. I have, in the last six weeks, come to understand what I lost by not believing the older woman. I do not want you to lose it too.*

*I am not going to sign my name because I do not know what your name is now. You may have married. You may have changed. You may not want to sign anything the way I would have.*

*But I have been you.*

*Do this for me.*

*— your younger self*

Meredith had, at the small round table, closed the letter.

She had put it back into its envelope.

She had, for a long moment, done nothing.

She had, at last, gotten up. She had walked into the small kitchen. She had, without particular thought, made a second pot of tea. She had come back to the sitting room. She had sat down.

She had, for the whole of that Tuesday evening, thought about the letter.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had spent eighteen years reading academic manuscripts, gone through several possible framings of what she had received.

The first was that it was a hoax. Someone, for reasons she could not identify, had produced a small clever hoax involving her younger handwriting, her real past address, a real small close-call incident from 2005, and a specific date in the current year. The hoax was, in this framing, meant to frighten her. It was — she considered this — well-executed. It was, in fact, so well-executed that she could not entirely identify who would have had the specific combination of resources and information required to produce it. She had, in the last decade, had few close friends. She had not, in her adult life, told anyone about the small close call with the brick. She had not, so far as she knew, ever mentioned Whiteladies Road, or the small pharmacy, or the specific fact of the hay fever antihistamine. The specific details in the letter were details only she could have known. If it was a hoax, it was a hoax by someone who had, at some point, been very deeply in her mind.

The second was that it was a mistake. That some other Meredith Cole, of Bristol, had received a similar letter from her own younger self, and that her letter had been mis-delivered. This was, on any inspection, absurd. But it was, as an explanation, less alarming than the alternatives.

The third was that it was a delusion. That she herself, in her long solitary life as a freelance editor, had produced the letter — that she had, in some sort of dissociative episode, written it herself and had, on receiving it, forgotten. This too was, on any inspection, unlikely. She had, throughout her adult life, been a woman of specific small careful mental habits, and had not, at any point, exhibited any tendency toward the kind of dissociation this framing required.

The fourth framing was that the letter was what it claimed to be.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman considering the impossible, considered this framing.

She had considered it, at some length, throughout the Tuesday evening. She had considered the specific claim — that some version of her at twenty-three had, in some way none of them had understood, been able to send a letter forward in time, addressed to a version of her at forty-four; that a similar letter had, in the past of that twenty-three-year-old, arrived from an eighty-eight-year-old version of herself; and that the whole arrangement was, so far as the letter suggested, the specific small system by which some future version of her was attempting to save the past versions from a small recurring point of failure.

She had considered, in that framing, what the specific mechanism might be. She had understood, considering it, that she had no specific mechanism to propose. She had considered whether the claim was, on its face, coherent. She had understood that it was — the claim was internally consistent in the small careful way of certain philosophical puzzles she had, at university, spent whole terms considering. It was not, in any specific sense, self-contradictory. It required only the acceptance of a specific small mechanism that she did not have.

She had considered, at last, what she would do if the letter were true.

She had considered this in the specific small honest way she had learned to consider difficult things.

She had understood, considering it, that the letter's specific request was small. It was asking her to do something different on the third of May. Anything different. Not to do anything specific. Not to sacrifice anything. Not to prevent anything. Only, on that specific day, to do something different from what she would ordinarily do.

She had understood that the cost of complying with the letter, if the letter were false, was very small. She would, on the third of May, take a slightly different route to the shops than usual. She would answer the telephone or not. She would cook something new for dinner. She would have, at the end of the day, spent a very small amount of additional effort in the specific small effort of doing something differently.

She had understood that the cost of not complying, if the letter were true, was her life.

She had considered this asymmetry for a long time.

She had, at eleven that Tuesday evening, understood the specific small careful truth about herself: that she was not, in the specific way of the letter's twenty-three-year-old, going to dismiss it.

She was going to do what the letter asked.

She was going to do this, she understood, not because she believed the letter's specific claim. She did not, on the whole, believe the letter's claim. She had understood over the course of the evening that no ordinary set of beliefs available to her permitted the letter's claim to be true. She was going to do it anyway. She was going to do it because the asymmetry made it obvious that she should. She was going to do it because it cost her almost nothing. And she was going to do it because, in some quiet way she did not entirely want to examine, she had believed the letter enough that the alternative — going through the third of May in the ordinary way, and then living for the following six weeks wondering whether some small thing she had not yet noticed was going to kill her — was, in the specific small honest way she understood herself, unbearable.

She had, at the small round table at eleven-thirty on the Tuesday evening, taken out her small notebook, and had written on the top of a fresh page:

*3 May. Do not do anything I would ordinarily do.*

She had underlined it.

She had gone to bed.

chapters.title: Fifth of May
chapters.body:
She had, over the following three weeks, thought about the letter perhaps ten thousand times.

She had not been able to prevent this. She had, on the Wednesday morning after receiving the letter, resolved to think about it only when necessary. She had discovered, by the Wednesday evening, that necessary was very frequent. She had thought about it while making coffee. She had thought about it while walking to the shop. She had thought about it while working, and while eating, and while going to bed, and while lying awake.

She had, over the three weeks, come to a small specific plan.

She was going to spend the third of May outside the flat. She was going to take a train, at seven in the morning, to a small town on the Welsh coast — a town she had never visited before, chosen at random from a small atlas one Sunday afternoon — and she was going to spend the day walking on the beach. She was going to eat her lunch at a specific small café she had identified on the internet. She was going to take the six o'clock train back to Bristol. She was going to be at home by nine.

She was, in short, going to spend the third of May doing something she had never done before, in a place she had never been before, following a small itinerary she had planned specifically to have no resemblance to anything she would ordinarily have done on a Tuesday in early May.

She had, on the morning of the third of May, gotten up at five-thirty. She had made her coffee. She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman about to take a train, packed a small bag. She had, at six-fifteen, walked to the small station.

She had taken the seven o'clock train.

She had arrived at the small Welsh town at ten-forty.

She had spent the day, in the specific small way she had planned, walking. The weather had been cold and clear. The beach had been almost empty. She had, at one, gone to the small café, and had eaten a small plate of fish and chips, and had drunk a small glass of white wine. She had, at three, walked back to the small station. She had waited for the six o'clock train. She had taken it. She had arrived at Bristol at eight-forty. She had walked home. She had, by nine, been at her flat.

She had, at nine-fifteen, made a small dinner she did not eat. She had, at nine-thirty, gotten into bed. She had, at nine-forty-five, turned off the light.

She had, in the dark, understood that she had, so far as she could tell, done nothing that she would have done in the ordinary way on the third of May.

She had, in the dark, tried to sleep.

She had, in the dark, understood that the specific test she had performed was a test whose result she could not, in any obvious way, know for six weeks.

She had, at last, slept.

—

She had, over the following six weeks, been very careful.

She had not, on the fourth of May or on any subsequent day, gone about her ordinary business with quite the same ordinary attention. She had watched, at every crossing, in every stairwell, on every walk, for the specific small quality of ordinary events that might, in some way she could not identify, become the specific event that would kill her. She had, over the six weeks, been aware of every small potential accident with a heightened, unsleeping attention.

Nothing had happened.

She had not been struck by a falling brick. She had not been hit by a car. She had not fallen. She had not had a small heart attack. She had not, in any specific way, come near to death.

She had, on the fourteenth of June — the specific date the letter had identified as her twenty-three-year-old self's death — sat at the small round table in her sitting room and had, at three in the afternoon, waited.

Nothing had happened at three.

Nothing had happened at four.

Nothing had happened at five.

At six she had made a small pot of tea. At seven she had eaten a small dinner. At eight she had sat in the small armchair by the window and had, for the first time in six weeks, permitted herself to consider the possibility that she had, by whatever small combination of small actions on the third of May, saved her own life.

She had considered this for a long time.

She had, at ten, gone to bed.

She had slept, that night, for the first time in six weeks, deeply.

—

She had, over the following months, tried to make sense of what had happened.

She had done this in the specific small careful way of a woman who did not, on the whole, believe in what she had just, apparently, done. She had considered, again, the possibility that the letter had been a hoax, and that she had, by taking it seriously, only inconvenienced herself for one day and had spent six weeks in unnecessary vigilance. She had considered the possibility that the letter had been genuine, but that the specific decision it had warned her about had, in fact, been made in the ordinary way — that she had, in some specific way she had not identified, still made the small fatal decision, and that its consequences had, for some small reason not visible to her, not appeared. She had considered the possibility that the letter had been genuine and that she had, by her small careful vigilance, actually saved herself.

She had not been able, in the specific small honest way of a woman considering these framings, to decide between them.

She had, over the months, come slowly to a small specific quiet peace with the fact that she was not going to know.

She had, however, decided to do one small thing.

She had, on the second of April in the year following the arrival of the letter, taken out the specific small notebook she had used to plan her small trip to Wales, and had, at the small round table, begun to write.

She had written a letter.

The letter had been addressed to *Meredith Cole,* and had been dated *2 April 2005.* Below the date, she had, in the specific small careful hand she had, over the intervening year, practiced to make more closely resemble the hand of her twenty-three-year-old self, begun:

*I am writing this on 2 April in the year 2026. I am forty-five. I am, at the moment of writing, alive.*

*I am writing to you on 2 April 2005 because I have understood, in the last year, that you are — that I was, at twenty-three — going to make a small decision on the third of May that would kill me. I have received, at forty-four, a letter from you. Your letter was postmarked 2 April 2005 and had been sent, so far as I can tell, from twenty-three to forty-four via some mechanism I do not understand. I have tested the mechanism, in the last year, in small careful ways. I have understood that if I put a letter into a small postbox on 2 April in the current year, addressed to myself at Gloucester Road in Bristol on 2 April 2005, it arrives.*

*I do not, on the whole, understand what I am doing.*

*I am writing to warn you.*

*You are, at twenty-three, going to receive a letter from an old woman who says she is you at eighty-eight. She is going to warn you that on 3 May 2005 you are going to make a small decision that will kill you. She is going to ask you to do something different that day. Anything different.*

*I am asking you the same thing.*

*Do not, on the third of May 2005, go to the pharmacy on Whiteladies Road. Do not walk home along your ordinary route. Go, instead, to the pharmacy on the other side of Bristol, at Bedminster. Walk home a different way. Do not, at three o'clock on that afternoon, be at the corner of Whiteladies and St Paul's Road.*

*I know this because I received your letter. Your letter told me that a brick fell at that corner and killed you. Your letter asked me, from the specific small position of a woman who had six weeks left, to do something different on the third of May of my forty-fourth year. I did. I am, at the time of writing, alive.*

*Do this for me.*

*I am not going to sign my name in the way you would recognize. But I have been you.*

*Do it.*

*— your older self*

She had, at the small round table, folded the letter into thirds. She had put it into a small white envelope. She had addressed it, in the specific small careful way, to *Miss Meredith Cole, 14 Gloucester Road, Bristol,* and had, on the return address line, left it blank.

She had, on the following morning, walked to a small postbox on the Gloucester Road that had, in fact, been the small postbox she had used, at twenty-three, for her ordinary post.

She had put the letter into the postbox.

She had walked home.

She had, that evening, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had done a small strange thing and did not know what to do with herself afterward, sat in the sitting room and had made herself a small cup of tea.

—

She had, over the years that followed, thought sometimes about what she had done.

She had, over those years, understood that she could not know whether her letter had arrived. She could not know whether the twenty-three-year-old had received it. She could not know whether the twenty-three-year-old — if the twenty-three-year-old had received it — had believed it, or had done what was asked, or had, in the six weeks after the third of May 2005, lived or died.

She had understood, in the small careful way of a woman who had made her peace with things she could not know, that this was, in the small specific arrangement of what she had done, going to have to be enough.

She had also, over the years, considered the specific small possibility that had, in some quiet way, remained with her.

The possibility was: that there was some woman, somewhere, at some age — perhaps at eighty-eight, perhaps at another age entirely — who was, or had been, or would be, the first Meredith. The one to whom no letter had come. The one who had, in the ordinary way of a small life, gone about her ordinary business on the third of May of her forty-fourth year, and had made her small ordinary decision, and had died. That woman, without the warning, had, in the specific small system of the letters, been the one whose death had, in some small way, initiated the whole small careful chain. She had, in her ordinary small forty-fourth year, done nothing to save herself; but she had, in her old age — perhaps only in some counterfactual old age Meredith could not describe — become the woman who had written the first letter to the first twenty-three-year-old, and had, in doing so, begun the small careful process of saving all the subsequent versions.

Meredith had, over the years, come to think that this first Meredith — whoever she had been, and however she had somehow written the first letter — was the specific small heroine of the whole business.

The first Meredith had, at eighty-eight, in some way Meredith could not entirely imagine, decided to do the small strange thing.

She had, in the specific small way of a woman doing a small strange thing that would help someone she would never meet, saved every subsequent Meredith.

Meredith had, in the small quiet of her sitting room at forty-five and forty-six and forty-seven, hoped that the first Meredith had, in her small last years, been at peace with what she had done.

She had, in the small quiet of her own life at forty-eight and forty-nine and fifty, become one of the Merediths who — in the small careful way of the specific chain the first Meredith had begun — was going to write the letter, from her own future old age, to the small twenty-three-year-old version of herself who would, in her time, need it.

She had understood that she was, in the small careful way of a woman inheriting a small careful responsibility, going to have to be careful to survive to eighty-eight, or however old she needed to be, so as to write the letter when it was time.

She had, over the years, understood that this was, in the specific small strange way, the whole content of her life.

She had lived carefully. She had done, in the small ordinary way of a Bristol editor, a small quiet responsible life. She had lived, in the years that followed, to eighty-nine.

She had, on 2 April of her eighty-ninth year, written the letter she had, throughout the last decades, been preparing to write.

She had, on the following morning, walked to the small postbox, and had, in the specific small careful way she had learned, posted it.

She had, that evening, sat in the small quiet of her sitting room, and had known that she had done what she had been asked to do.

She had, in the specific small way of a woman who had, at last, closed the small circle she had, at forty-four, been asked to close, been at peace.

She had, at eighty-nine, died in her sleep some months later, in the same small flat on Alma Road she had lived in for the whole of her adult life.

The letter she had written, so far as anyone knows, arrived at 2 April 2005 in the small postbox of the small student flat on Gloucester Road, and was, in the small careful way of Meredith Cole at twenty-three, read.

Whether the twenty-three-year-old had, on that morning, believed it, and had, on the third of May, done something different, is not, on the whole, the sort of thing anyone alive is in a position to know.

The circle, in the small quiet way of the circles Meredith had been part of, has gone on going.

Somewhere, in some year, the small letter is still being written.

Somewhere, in some year, it is still being received.
